7 Reasons The Death Of The Sedan Has Been Greatly Exaggerated

TB
By Tyler Brooks Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead • via Jalopnik Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Jalopnik Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights
  • Jalopnik readers tell automakers to make more sedans , yet despite the obvious enthusiast demand, it felt for a while like the traditional four-door car was destined for a niche fate like station wagons and landline telephones.
  • But something funny has happened on the way to the sedan's funeral: Americans are buying them again.
  • Official reporting verified via Jalopnik news desk.
⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • TYLER BROOKS Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead

Automotive Innovation & Market Feasibility

Concept prototypes and viral vehicle reveals offer an exciting window into the automotive industry's future design language. Dispatches from Jalopnik demonstrate how radical styling, lightweight materials, and powertrain packaging can transition from design studios to production assembly lines. Engineering feasibility and homologation standards remain the true measures of impact.

Big Picture: Market reception and formal OEM production announcements will determine which concept innovations make it to consumer streets.

Jalopnik readers tell automakers to make more sedans , yet despite the obvious enthusiast demand, it felt for a while like the traditional four-door car was destined for a niche fate like station wagons and landline telephones. But something funny has happened on the way to the sedan's funeral: Americans are buying them again.

📌 The Core Development

They never really stopped, of course. Nobody considers the Camry and the Accord to be endangered species, but on the other hand, we have other manufacturers abandoning the segment completely. Sales figures from 2026 have shown interest in sedans on the uptick across multiple brands and price ranges. The crossoverfication of the market will likely continue, but perhaps reports of the sedan's inevitable demise have been overstated.

This shift is obviously welcome, but today we're going to dig into what may be behind it, what's going on with SUVs, and whether the year's lift in sales is an anomalous blip or the beginning of a sedan resurgence.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

For a minute there, it felt like every bit of automotive news about the American sedan market was about another model being discontinued, a factory switching over to SUV production, or an automaker explaining why nobody wants a regular car anymore. Sales figures for the first nine months of 2026 tell a different story, however. The Toyota Camry sold 260,684 units through September, up 11.2% over the same period in 2025. The Honda Accord was up even more, with a 32.7% increase. What about down market? The Corolla was up 8.4% and the Civic by 5.4%. These aren't obscure enthusiast darlings. They were once the bread and butter of the entire car market, now showing some momentum again.

These numbers are interesting, but they wouldn't necessarily mean a whole lot in isolation. If you take Honda as an example, though, passenger cars in general were up by 16.5% through September, while trucks and SUVs were essentially flat, actually declining by 0.3%. It's almost like sedans are poised to make a comeback . But why?

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

One of the big reasons why sedans may be gaining traction again has nothing to do with sedans. Conventional wisdom has long held that Americans were willing to pay extra for the privilege of sitting really high in traffic. But a market where the cheapest new full-sized SUVs start at more than $60,000 , combined with an economic crunch that has become hard to ignore, is making SUV math look more and more unappealing.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

Kelley Blue Book data helps show just how stark the choice has become. Looking at transaction prices, the cost of a new compact car has been $27,977 on average. To step up into a compact SUV, that average jumps to $37,614. For a mid-size SUV, it's $50,630. We aren't talking about full-sized SUVs that dramatically increase seating and cargo capacity for that money, so buyers are paying that sort of premium for a vehicle configuration that's potentially very similar.

Cars actually asked Hyundai about this, and the brand confirmed that affordability was driving this shift, with fuel economy and the overall perception of value playing roles as well. So, while a sedan may sit lower and offer a bit less space inside, it's also delivering a lower price tag and better gas mileage without asking anyone to give up a trunk and a proper back seat.
